stories.head: EU Space Act could bog down industry growth.
stories.body: European space industry experts are warning that the EU Space Act may introduce bureaucratic hurdles that could stifle competitiveness. As the space race heats up globally, this legislation could prove to be more of a hindrance than a help. The irony is that while the EU aims to bolster its space industry, it may inadvertently be creating red tape that rivals the complexity of rocket science.
stories.soWhat: If the EU wants to play in the big leagues, it might want to streamline its regulations instead of adding layers that could ground innovation.

stories.head: SpinLaunch eyes opportunity amid geopolitical shifts.
stories.body: SpinLaunch's CEO has identified geopolitical changes as a potential growth avenue for the space sector. The company, known for its kinetic launch technology, sees a chance to capitalize on the shifting dynamics of international relations, suggesting that sometimes the best launchpad is a political one. This could be a savvy move in a landscape where traditional launch methods face increasing scrutiny.
stories.soWhat: If SpinLaunch can navigate the political landscape as deftly as it does its launches, it might just redefine how we think about entry into orbit.

stories.head: Kongsberg NanoAvionics aims for sovereign constellations.
stories.body: Kongsberg NanoAvionics has set its sights on building and supporting sovereign satellite constellations after securing a significant contract. This move underscores a growing trend where nations are prioritizing self-sufficiency in space capabilities. As governments look to bolster their own space assets, Kongsberg is positioning itself as a key player in a market that could see increased demand for national pride over partnership.
stories.soWhat: If Kongsberg's gamble pays off, we might see a resurgence of nationalistic space programs that could reshape the competitive landscape.

talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
